doc.title: Donn Andre interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, June 6, 2009

title: The rhythm section must know the tunes
summary: Why rhythm players and drummers must know the changes.

story.theme_name: Drummers and drumming: who played what, and how
story.community_name: Great drummers: who they admired and why

blocks.x: When you get in a situation, I mean I always felt like the rhythm players, the bass and the guitar and the banjo — how do I put this — you have to know a song better than the horn players. That’s how I felt in that situation. Because horn players can find single notes, they can sort of meander their way through things, but you guys have to play the correct changes and stuff.

Oh yeah that’s very true. The rhythm section, even the drummer. I judge the quality of a drummer by the way that he plays the tune, the accents that he puts in at the right place at the right time. And some drummers are good drummers but they just don’t have a feel for the music or they don’t know the tune. But as far as people who are doing notes, like me, the chords, Gordy on the tuba, or the bass player, you really have to know the tune pretty well. Because if you don’t play the right changes you can throw the lead horn off something terribly. And I have a friend that says when I do on salad sometimes sounds like chord salad. When I’m doing chords sometimes I screw them up so badly that it sounds like chord salad.
Well if you have a good bass player or tuba man, and you can rely on them hitting that downbeat note, but if they’re not then it can be hairy.
That’s absolutely right. Sometimes you know you’re both feeding off of each other and if you both don’t know the tune very well it’s not fun.
